newsitem.title: USA: U.S. cash crude prices lower as refiners hold off.
newsitem.headline: U.S. cash crude prices lower as refiners hold off.

text.p: U.S. cash crudes prices were starting Monday weaker as ample supply and the prospects that Iraq will hit the market again shortly encouraged refiners to hold off buying, trades said.
"Refiners are all meeting this morning and I don't think you're going to see much getting done," said a Houston broker.
Among early trades was a Midland/West Texas Intermediate at a 30 cent disount to benchmark Cushing/WTI, a little changed differential against a lower outright price compared with late last week.
WTI started firmer outright on Monday but soon turned lower and was down 13 cents at $19.45 just before noon (the Exchange for Physical premium was unchanged at around two cents).
"We're taking a wait-and-see attitude," said a trader for a large independent refiner.

"The Far East has been snatching some Brents away and the word we're getting is that there may not be as much Brent coming out (in August). That's been keeping a floor under it but there is still plenty of crude around," the trader said.
Light Louisiana Sweet/St. James, Brent's closest domestic competitor, remained fairly firm at an 18/20 cent premium, but with little trading interest seen.
The weaker market was reflected in a steeper contango, around 15 cents for August versus September, compared with nine cents late last week.
West Texas Sour/Midland was around $1.12/$1.18 under WTI, little changed from late last week.

The timing for the restart of Iraq's exports under its "oil-for-food" scheme with the United Nations remained the "wild card" for the market, said one trader. Last week, the U.N. coordinator said the key element for restarting exports, the aid distribution plan, was near to being completed.
Traders also are awaiting this week's reports on inventories and refinery utilization from the Department of Energy and the American Petroleum Institute, due out Wednesday and Tuesday, respectively.
Refinery runs nationwide have come off very high levels in the past two weeks. But despite weaker product margins refineries continue to operate in the high 90s percent of capacity.

"Margins are not as good as they have been but we are not cutting back on runs," said an Oklahoma crude trader for a medium-sized integrated oil company. But he said that there was still a good choice of crude available at fairly cheap levels.
